extracted.intended_audience: actors, comedians, improvisers, and performers learning to improve comedic timing
extracted.subtask_short: comedic timing for actors and comedians
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance for performers (actors, standup, sketch, improv) on using pauses, cadence, pacing, and delivery to land jokes and shape comedic scenes. Focuses on techniques, practice habits, and stylistic choices that improve how jokes and reactions register with an audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of pauses, cadence, delivery, and pacing
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedic timing is the use of pauses, cadence, delivery, and pacing to land a joke; the tempo of acting choices affects a single gag or a full comedic scene.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes examples of the 'pregnant pause' and contrasts between slow timing (pregnant pauses, Joe Pera) and fast zippy screwball dialogue (I Love Lucy candy factory episode). Emphasizes that timing is a composite of pause placement, cadence, and delivery choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pregnant pause before the punchline
rubrics_metrics.description: Place a pregnant pause at the end of a joke (right before the punchline) to build suspense and anticipation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classic technique used by Henny Youngman, Jack Benny, and Sacha Baron Cohen; recommended as the simplest foundational technique to master before trying more complex timing. Practice reveals if pauses are too long or too short.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match timing to style and character
rubrics_metrics.description: Timing should be geared toward whatever suits you (or your character) best — slow or fast pacing depending on voice, persona, and genre.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: slow, stammering Joe Pera vs. rapid screwball comedy. Consider the comedian/character more than the joke itself and adapt timing to fit persona and contemporary tastes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perfecting delivery via rhythm and musicality
rubrics_metrics.description: Your timing affects how every joke lands; find a rhythm in material like music to know where laughs and pauses belong.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Developed over repeated performance. Quote: 'After I do a joke or a bit for a long time, it’s got a rhythm; I know where the laughs are coming or where the pauses are.' Listen for rises in voice and musicality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Set audience expectations through pauses
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a pause to give the audience time to form an expectation so you can subvert it with the punchline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Subverting expectations is a common joke format and requires giving listeners time to predict so the reversal lands. The pause is what allows the audience to consider and then be surprised.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow time for audience reaction; avoid running over laughs
rubrics_metrics.description: Find the right pacing by letting the audience get the joke and laugh before continuing; 'running over laughs' is a sign of nervousness or inexperience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practically, pause after laughs to let them breathe; learn to read audience energy and not rush into the next line.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practice in front of people and experiment
rubrics_metrics.description: Hone timing by performing for real audiences; play off their energy, develop rhythm, and try variations to see what works.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Options include standup, improv classes, small gatherings, or informal practice. Quote: 'It can take thousands of shows to figure it out. Experiment [during] every show to see what works best.' Take notes on what succeeds and fails.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study widely across comedy forms
rubrics_metrics.description: Soak up many types of comedy to absorb timing styles and rhythms — from multicam sitcoms to silent film physicality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare shows like 'Friends' (multicam) vs 'Modern Family' (single-cam), watch Buster Keaton, Charlie Chaplin, and a wide array of standup comics. 'You absorb [comedic timing]' by exposure to varied sensibilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the text — mark beats and choices
rubrics_metrics.description: When working from a script, study it and note what makes you laugh, where pauses or beats are written, and what delivery choices the words suggest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sometimes the page won't be funny until your delivery makes it so: note explicit beats/pauses, choose where to emphasize consonants, and let textual clues guide timing. Example: Jerry Seinfeld breaking down which words in a joke are 'funny.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow joke format: place pause before punchline in setup-punchline structure
rubrics_metrics.description: If telling a standard setup-and-punchline joke, the easiest place to pause is right before the punchline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The pregnant pause is highlighted as the 'simple equation' to master; practice will show appropriate pause length and whether it lands or drags.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use pauses to let information sink in for character and audience
rubrics_metrics.description: In scenes, use pauses to allow both the character and audience to process information — especially important for the straight man reacting to outlandish behavior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pauses serve an in-world function (character comprehension) and an audience-facing one. This technique underpins many reaction-based punchlines where the response is the joke.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study masters and read comedy literature
rubrics_metrics.description: Learn timing strategies by studying comedians' work and reading books on improvisation, joke-telling, and comedy writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resources include biographies, interviews, and craft books that explain how prominent comedians developed rhythm and style; use these to inform your own timing choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write out subtext to inform pause length
rubrics_metrics.description: Make note of what you or your character is thinking during pauses to determine how long those pauses should be.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sitting with material and articulating subtext gives a practical yardstick for pause duration — it makes pauses motivated rather than arbitrary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Listen and stay in the moment with scene partners
rubrics_metrics.description: Stay present and listen to partners so pauses and reactions feel natural rather than forced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Being attentive lets timing evolve organically in performance; this makes laughs feel earned and not trotted out mechanically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use reaction and physicality as part of timing
rubrics_metrics.description: Combine pauses with physical comedy and reactions; sometimes the reaction (and its timing) becomes the punchline itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical examples: Jack Benny's reaction to interruption, Gene Wilder combining pause with physical business, and 'The Office' using reaction as the joke. Integrate movement and facial expression into timing choices.
